# Things-MCP

House rules: github.com/mathiswrong/control, local copy in `_control/` beside the project folders. The global rules in `~/.codex/AGENTS.md` apply here as well.

## Status ledger

`STATUS.md` at this repo root is the session ledger, one `## <task>` entry per piece of work in flight (format: `_control/templates/STATUS.md`). Before ending a session, add or update your own entry: tool, model, state (working, blocked, waiting on me, or done), last touched, next step. Leave other sessions' entries alone. No secrets, tokens, or private links in it.

## Rules in force

### Web deploys

The repo is the deploy spine. Vercel and Railway build production from main, staging from preview branches. No CLI-only deploys as a steady state.

Pushing to a linked repo is deploying. Once a project is wired up, push is not a safe "just save my work" action. Say this out loud before pushing to a linked repo, and do not push a site to production without Paul's explicit go unless this repo's local rules grant default deploy authority.

Never deploy application source by local upload (`railway up`, `railway deployment up`, a directory push). A production deploy must be attributable to a GitHub commit. The CLI is fine for read-only work: logs, metrics, config, incident response. If a local upload is ever found in production, do not redeploy it: reconcile the code into GitHub, pass CI, and replace it with a GitHub-triggered deploy.

After a deploy, confirm it took. Hit a real endpoint, or check a version, timestamp, or heartbeat. Do not eyeball the dashboard. For Railway, confirm every service reached SUCCESS and that each deployment's commitHash equals the new main SHA.

Set every env var in both Preview and Production scope in the same step. Workers that are not leader-locked stay at one replica. One-off production scripts run through the platform's own environment (`railway run ...`) so secrets are never handled by hand.

### Web security baseline

- User-scoped data access in exactly one layer, with IDOR tests.
- Sanitize at import and at render (DOMPurify or equivalent).
- Strict CSP and HSTS. Inline scripts are hashed into the CSP, never `unsafe-inline`.
- Buckets are never public. Attachments move only by short-lived presigned URLs, never proxied through the API.
- Audit log for auth, export, and delete events.
- Schema changes only through migrations. Never hand-edit a production schema.
- Business logic server side only. Prices, entitlements, and limits are decided by the server.
- Local-first reads where the product promises it: the UI reads an on-device mirror, connectivity is how data arrives. The airplane-mode test is the acceptance bar.

### Telemetry

Sentry in every part of the app: client, native, server, worker. Same-origin tunnel on web. No other third-party trackers, fonts, or analytics from the client. GA4 only on a marketing apex, never inside the product. A project's local rules may narrow this further (for example a site with no analytics at all); they never widen it without Paul's say.

### Security checklist, before any release

Run the full pass before any real release: first launch, and any time auth, payments, or user data handling changes. Ordered by how often each one bites.

1. Access control. Change an ID in a URL or API call and try to read another user's data (IDOR). Being logged in is not being allowed. A revoked or deleted user loses access on the next request, not at next login. Try admin-only routes as a normal user.
2. Secrets. Search the client bundle for keys. Env vars split correctly between server-only and public. Keychain items `WhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly`; on-device databases under `NSFileProtectionComplete`.
3. Injection and XSS. Script tags and SQL-ish strings into every input. Queries parameterized, rendered user content sanitized.
4. Business logic stays server side. Watch the network tab during checkout: price and entitlement come from the server response.
5. Configuration. No stack traces in production error pages, no default credentials or debug routes, no `USING (true)` database policies. CSP and HSTS present.
6. Dependencies. `npm audit` or the platform equivalent; patch known CVEs before shipping.
7. Auth and rate limiting. Hit your own API in a loop and confirm the limiter stops you, and that it is live in production, not behind an unset env var. Sessions expire and are revoked on password reset.
8. Webhook integrity. Every webhook handler (Stripe, Resend, anything else) verifies the signature before trusting the event. This one bites Resend and Stripe integrations specifically.
9. Logging and recovery. Auth failures and errors reach Sentry on client and server. Backups exist and one has actually been restored at least once.
10. SSRF. Anywhere the app fetches a user-provided URL (feeds, importers, link previews, avatars), confirm it cannot reach internal addresses or private ranges.
11. Abuse and concurrency. Submit the same form twice fast. Edit one record as two users. Upload an oversized file to every upload field. Fan-outs use bounded concurrency with per-item error isolation.
12. Data basics. The main list is one query, not one per row. An index on everything filtered or sorted. Test with an empty database.

House additions: no third-party trackers, fonts, or analytics from the client; privacy manifest, App Privacy answers, and the privacy page say the same thing; support can act on the Support ID the app shows; no disposable media, AI relics, secrets, `.env` files, or stale branches in the tree.

Never write "I checked everything and it's secure." Write what you tested, what you found, and what is still unverified. Quote the actual error.

### Release check, an hour not a night

Paul, October 2, 2026: a build should not take all night to mint. Before merging to main on a repo that deploys from it, or before minting a native build:

1. Typecheck, unit tests, and the production build pass (native: the unit test scheme, plus the app builds for macOS and an iPhone or iPad simulator).
2. One hands-on pass of the real app on the screens the change touches, at the sizes it ships, on synthetic data or a staging fixture: create and edit, reopen, navigate between the main containers, open Settings and return, search.
3. Look at every screen the change touched, in light and dark: text reads, weights and hierarchy make sense, nothing is bunched up or pushed into a corner, counts sit on one edge.

Do not test every permutation of every option. Run the full smoke suite only when the change touches sync, storage, sign-in, or the editor bridge, or before an App Store submission. Say what you checked in the PR or build notes. Keep fixture accounts on staging and preserve installed user data. A broken core workflow (write, save, reopen, navigate, search) still blocks the build.

### Design process, before any new surface

For anything with real product shape (a new screen, a new flow, not a one-line copy fix), do not start in code. First write down what the surface is for in one sentence, the states it handles (loading, empty, populated, error, at minimum), and the existing pattern it should match. Get a look at the plan before anything gets built.

Mock a genuinely new surface before coding it: artboards for macOS first, then iPhone and iPad, in both colorways, and get approval. Existing surfaces are reviewed and improved in the real app with its real controls, not in substitute mockups.

Decide the system once, not per screen: a small fixed set of color tokens, one typeface family with a handful of sizes, one spacing base unit. Hierarchy comes from type weight, size, and spacing before it reaches for a new color.

Use the platform's own components. A custom-built control quietly loses accessibility, keyboard support, and consistent behavior.

Every list has four states, designed on purpose. Check a well-made product's version of the same screen before calling a design done. Write real copy, never placeholder copy.

Scale to the task: a routine styling fix is not a research project. Say plainly when the right answer is "this is small, ship it."

# Project working rules

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Open Things 3 before launching your LLM client.**
>
> Things must already be running on the Mac hosting Things MCP before you open your AI app or browser conversation. Otherwise, you may see **“unable to connect to server”**. Keep Things running while you use the connection.
>
> **Already seeing the error?** Open Things, fully quit and reopen your desktop client (or reload your browser client), then start a new conversation and check the connection.

This startup order applies to live connections. Automated builds and tests do not require Things or an LLM client.

- Follow `CONTRIBUTING.md` for portable build, verification, and contribution requirements.
- Use neutral `feat/` or `fix/` branches. Keep commit messages, pull requests, comments, and docstrings technical and free of provenance signatures or automated co-author trailers. Name integrations only where needed for compatibility or required configuration. Preserve legally required third-party notices.
- Keep credentials, task data, personal configuration, private conversations, screenshots, disposable outputs, and builds out of source control. Scan the tree, reachable history, release assets, and pull-request text before publication.
- Use only supported Things automation. Never write to its database, use private experimental APIs, collect Things Cloud credentials, or expose generic script execution.
- No Apple Shortcuts dependency, bridge, or installation. Keep the server lightweight. If Things has no supported mechanism for an operation, document the limit and omit it; do not implement substitute schedulers or workflows. Native repeat-rule editing is excluded on that basis.
- Retain shared state, locking, durable request IDs, revision checks, and read-back verification across clients. Never retry an uncertain mutation automatically.
- New installations default to read-only. Enable a library owner's normal client grants only when they request write access. For authorized live verification, mutate one clearly labeled synthetic item at a time and read it back before continuing. Destructive tests require a disposable library.
- Keep the local core usable without a project-operated account or hosted service. Optional remote providers must remain replaceable. Builds and tests must not require personal credentials, signing identities, or private services.
- Use maintained dependencies and preserve redistribution requirements. Do not redistribute Things or proprietary vendor assets.
- Product planning precedes implementation. New UI requires approved designs. There is no companion app, custom setup window, or menu-bar app. Prefer existing client installation and settings controls. Document advanced setup honestly when a command-free installation is unavailable.
- Run appropriate local checks and update the pull request. Do not merge, change visibility, publish packages, or grant a license without the owner's explicit authorization.
- Consult `almanac/` for architecture and historical decisions. Current code takes precedence over historical descriptions. Treat the wiki as read-only during ordinary development; use its maintenance workflow for wiki changes.

## What this is

Find and manage Things 3 tasks from a conversation. Things MCP connects compatible MCP clients to the Things app on your Mac through its supported automation in
